name: Cardinale
description: A Negroni with dry vermouth in place of sweet. Drier, paler, and sharper at the finish.
funFact: The name is usually traced to the Hotel Excelsior in Rome, where a cardinal is said to have asked for his Negroni without the sweetness.

steps: Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds until properly cold and diluted.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish and serve.

name: Pirlo
description: Still white wine with Campari poured through it and a splash of soda. Brescia's own aperitivo, older than the Venetian spritz.
funFact: The name comes from the Brescian dialect verb pirlare, to spin — the Campari corkscrews down through the wine as it is poured, which is the whole trick.

steps: Fill a wine glass with ice and add the white wine.
Pour the Campari slowly into the centre so it spirals down through the wine.
Add a small splash of soda.
Do not stir it flat — the descending swirl is the point.

name: Hugo
description: Prosecco, elderflower, mint and lime over ice. The Alpine answer to the Aperol Spritz, and lighter than any of them.
funFact: Roland Gruber mixed the first one in Naturns in 2005 and used lemon balm syrup; elderflower only replaced it once the drink spread beyond South Tyrol.

steps: Put the mint and lime wedges in a large wine glass and press them once, gently.
Add the elderflower syrup and fill the glass with ice.
Pour in the prosecco, then top with soda water.
Stir once from the bottom and serve with the mint standing proud.
recipe.garnish: A mint sprig and a lime wedge

name: Kaisermelange
description: Black coffee whisked with an egg yolk and honey, laced with brandy. A Viennese coffee house order, not a bar one.
funFact: Viennese coffee houses run to dozens of named preparations, each with a fixed ratio of coffee to milk to foam — ordering simply a coffee marks you out immediately.

steps: Whisk the egg yolk with the honey until pale and smooth.
Pour a little of the hot coffee in slowly while whisking, to temper the yolk.
Add the brandy and the rest of the coffee, whisking as you go.
Serve in a warmed glass without straining.

name: Kafi Luz
description: Weak coffee with a serious measure of fruit brandy. The house drink of central Swiss village taverns.
funFact: It is traditionally poured pale on purpose — the coffee is there to carry the Träsch, the pear-and-apple brandy of central Switzerland, rather than the other way round.

steps: Stir the sugar into the hot coffee until it dissolves.
Add the Trasch and stir once more.
Serve in a small handled glass, hot.
Refills are poured into the same glass without rinsing it.

name: Eierpunsch
description: Hot white wine beaten with egg yolks, sugar and vanilla until thick. The richest thing at a German Christmas market.
funFact: Christmas market stalls sell it in the same returnable ceramic mug as Glühwein, and the deposit on the mug is often larger than the drink.

steps: Whisk the yolks, sugar and vanilla in a bowl until pale.
Heat the wine to just below a simmer, never letting it boil.
Pour the hot wine onto the yolks in a thin stream, whisking constantly.
Return to a low heat and whisk until it thickens enough to coat a spoon.
Pour into a warmed mug and serve at once.

name: Maibowle
description: White wine infused with sweet woodruff and topped with sparkling wine. Made once a year, in May, when the herb is young.
funFact: The woodruff has to be picked before it flowers and wilted for a day first — fresh green leaves give nothing, and too much of it turns the punch bitter.

steps: Wilt the woodruff for a day, then tie it in a bunch by the stems.
Hang it in the white wine with the cut ends clear of the liquid and steep for no more than 30 minutes.
Lift out the herb and stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Chill thoroughly, then add the sparkling wine just before serving.
recipe.garnish: A woodruff sprig and a few strawberries

name: Diesel
description: Lager and cola, half and half. Ordered without irony in every German pub, and darker than either half suggests.
funFact: The same mix goes by different names depending on the beer and the region — Krefelder with Altbier, Colaweizen with wheat beer, and Diesel almost everywhere else.

steps: Chill both thoroughly.
Pour the cola into a tilted pint glass first.
Add the beer slowly down the side to keep the head from running over.
Serve without stirring.

name: Kaffekask
description: Coffee and brännvin in the same cup, measured by whether you can see a coin at the bottom.
funFact: The traditional measure is a coin dropped in the empty cup: pour coffee until it disappears, then pour spirit until you can see it again.

steps: Drop a small coin into the bottom of the cup if you are doing it properly.
Pour hot coffee until the coin is no longer visible.
Add brannvin until the coin comes back into view.
Sweeten if you like, and drink it hot.

name: Svařák
description: Czech mulled wine: red wine warmed with cloves, cinnamon and citrus, and poured by the litre at winter markets.
funFact: Czech svařák is usually poured far less sweet than German Glühwein, and market stalls heat it in open vats rather than sealed urns.

steps: Combine everything in a wide pan.
Heat slowly to steaming and hold it there for 20 minutes without boiling.
Taste and add sugar only if it needs it.
Ladle into warmed mugs, spices and all.

name: Hriatô
description: Caramelised sugar, pork fat and borovicka, drunk hot. A mountain drink that makes no apology for any of that.
funFact: It comes from the shepherding regions of Liptov and Orava, where the fat was the point — it was a working drink for cold weather, not a novelty.

steps: Melt the sugar in a small pan until it caramelises to a deep amber.
Add the lard and let it melt into the caramel.
Pour in the water carefully — it will spit — and stir until smooth.
Take it off the heat, add the spirit, and serve hot with a slice of bread.

name: Šumadijski Čaj
description: Serbian tea, which contains no tea. Rakija heated with sugar and honey until it looks entirely innocent.
funFact: The name is the joke: it arrives the colour of tea, in a tea glass, and is drunk in tea-sized sips for reasons that become clear quickly.

steps: Caramelise the sugar in a small pan until amber.
Add the water and stir until the caramel dissolves again.
Pour in the rakija and warm it through without letting it boil off.
Stir in the honey and serve hot in a small glass.

name: Arak Limonana
description: Frozen mint lemonade with arak poured through it. The drink Tel Aviv runs on between May and October.
funFact: Limonana is a coined word — limon plus nana, lemon plus mint — invented for an Israeli advertising campaign in the 1990s that sold a drink which did not exist yet.

steps: Blend the lemon juice, mint, syrup and ice until slushy and bright green.
Pour into a tall glass.
Pour the arak over the top and watch it turn the surface milky.
Serve with a spoon and a straw.

name: Poktanju
description: A shot glass of soju or whisky dropped into a glass of beer, and drunk in one go. The bomb drink.
funFact: Poktanju is the dropped version and somaek the poured one — the distinction matters at a Korean table, where the pouring itself carries a full set of manners.

steps: Pour the beer into a glass, leaving room at the top.
Rest a filled shot glass on the rim, or drop it in from a height.
Let it settle for a second — it will foam hard.
Drink it down in one, which is not optional.

name: Subak Soju
description: A hollowed watermelon filled with its own blended flesh and soju, and served back in the rind.
funFact: It is sold that way in Korean pubs — the emptied melon comes to the table as the vessel, with ladles, and is shared between four or more people.

steps: Cut the top off the watermelon and scoop out the flesh, keeping the shell whole.
Blend the flesh smooth and strain out the seeds.
Stir the juice together with the soju and pour it back into the shell.
Add ice and serve with a ladle and several glasses.
recipe.garnish: The watermelon lid, set back on top

name: Arak Attack
description: Balinese arak with orange juice and a red float. The cheapest drink on Bali and the one most travellers meet first.
funFact: Balinese arak is distilled from palm sap or rice and varies wildly by producer, which is why the orange juice is doing more work than it appears to be.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the arak and top with orange juice.
Stir once to combine.
Trickle the grenadine down the inside so it settles at the bottom.

name: Arrack Sour
description: Ceylon coconut arrack with lime and sugar. A sour built on a spirit made from the sap of a flower.
funFact: Sri Lankan arrack is distilled from the sap of unopened coconut flowers, tapped by climbers who move between treetops on ropes strung across the canopy.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish and serve immediately.

name: Bandera
description: Three glasses in a row — lime, blanco tequila and sangrita — arranged in the colours of the Mexican flag.
funFact: It is not a shot to be thrown back: the order is meant to be sipped in rotation, and the sangrita is the chaser, never the mixer.

steps: Line up three shot glasses left to right.
Fill the first with lime juice, the second with blanco tequila, the third with sangrita.
Sip from each in turn rather than drinking any of them down.
Refill whichever empties first.

name: Batida
description: Cachaça blended with fruit and sweetened condensed milk until it is thick enough to stand a straw in.
funFact: Batida simply means shaken, and the form takes any fruit at all — coconut, passion fruit, tamarind, cashew fruit — with condensed milk as the constant.

steps: Put everything in a blender.
Blend until completely smooth and thick.
Pour into a tall glass without straining.
Serve with a wide straw.

name: Ponche a la Romana
description: Sparkling wine poured over pineapple ice cream. Chile drinks it at New Year and at every national holiday.
funFact: The name points at Rome and the drink has nothing to do with it — the Chilean version fixed on pineapple ice cream and never looked back.

steps: Put two scoops of pineapple ice cream in a wide chilled glass.
Pour the sparkling wine slowly over the top so it foams up but does not spill.
Let it sit for a moment until the ice cream starts to soften at the edges.
Serve with both a spoon and a straw.

name: Papelón con Limón y Ron
description: Raw cane sugar dissolved in water with lime, poured over ice and cut with rum.
funFact: Papelón is unrefined cane sugar sold in solid cones; it has to be dissolved in warm water first, and it tastes nothing like white sugar syrup.

steps: Dissolve the grated papelon in the warm water and let it cool completely.
Add the lime juice and stir.
Fill a tall glass with ice and pour the mixture over.
Add the rum and stir once more.

name: Rum and Ting
description: Overproof white rum with Ting, the Jamaican grapefruit soda. Two ingredients, no ceremony.
funFact: Ting is made with real grapefruit juice and is bracingly bitter, which is the only reason it can stand up to 63 percent rum.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the rum.
Top with cold Ting.
Stir once and add a squeeze of lime if the soda is very sweet.

name: Ponche de Crème
description: Trinidad's Christmas drink: eggs, condensed milk, rum and a heavy hand with the Angostura.
funFact: Angostura bitters have been made in Trinidad since 1875, and in a Ponche de Creme they are a measured ingredient rather than a dash.

steps: Beat the eggs with the lime zest until completely smooth and pale.
Whisk in both milks, then the rum, then the bitters.
Strain through a fine sieve to catch the zest and any thread of egg.
Chill for at least a day before serving — it thickens and settles as it rests.
Serve cold, over one cube of ice, with nutmeg over the top.

name: Springbok
description: Green crème de menthe under a layer of Amarula, poured to the colours of the national rugby jersey.
funFact: Amarula is made from the fruit of the marula tree, which grows wild across southern Africa and is harvested from the ground rather than picked.

steps: Pour the crème de menthe into a shot glass.
Rest a barspoon just above the surface, curve up.
Pour the Amarula slowly over the back of it so it floats in a clean layer.
Serve without disturbing the line between them.

name: Sour de Maracuyá
description: A Pisco Sour rerouted through passion fruit. Sharper, more floral, and harder to stop at one.
funFact: Peruvian pisco is never diluted or aged in wood after distillation, so the fruit in a sour has nothing to hide behind.

steps: Dry-shake everything but the bitters, without ice, for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard until the tin frosts.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe and let the foam settle.
Drop three dashes of Angostura onto the foam.
recipe.garnish: Three drops of Angostura bitters on the foam
